item.title: How the midterm results could impact your taxes, housing and everyday prices
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
(Bloomberg) -- Americans handed Democrats a thumping midterm victory on Tuesday, and with it, a mandate to fix their money problems. In survey after survey, voters voiced their anger over the state of the US economy, especially the cost of essentials like food, gas and housing. Most Read from Bloomberg Morgan Stanley Offers $2.3 Billion Debt for Dell Family Deal Democrats Clinch Huge Wins on Inflation Anger, Trump Fatigue What the Democrats’ Sweep of Congress Means for Trump Democrats Sweep to Control of Congress in Rebuke of Trump Trump Now Has to Govern Through a Midterm Meltdown of His Own Making Many voters now expect their newly elected leaders to do something to lower the cost of living and help them save. But it's rarely that simple. Congress can't control markets and GDP growth, much less gas prices and groceries. And while candidates have pledged to push back on tariffs and the Iran war, much still lies in President Donald Trump's control. Nevertheless, elections matter, and the results could have long-term consequences in areas like taxes, retirement, AI regulation and more. Here is what the reversal of power in Congress could mean for your personal balance sheet. Taxes Trump’s signature economic accomplishment was last year’s passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Democrats won’t be able to unwind the bill’s major provisions, like tax cuts for high earners, since Trump has veto power over legislation. They could act to extend some of the OBBBA’s temporary provisions that they favor, according to Alvina Lo, head of advice, planning and fiduciary services at BNY Wealth. Those temporary provisions include deductions for a portion of overtime pay and tip income, as well as an additional deduction for taxpayers aged 65 and older. Also on the table is the status of the state and local tax, or SALT, deduction, which is set to revert from its current $40,000 cap to its prior level of $10,000 at the end of 2029. Some Democrats from high-tax states like New York and New Jersey have called for eliminating the SALT cap entirely. Some state and local results may also have national implications. In California, voters appeared on track to defeat a tax on billionaire wealth and approved a measure making a higher marginal tax rate permanent. That suggests a broad wealth tax like the one floated by Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren and others is unlikely, Lo said, though there’s an appetite at the state level to raise marginal tax rates. Those moves could give wealthy Americans continued reason to leave high-tax states. Those who can’t move will likely keep setting up trusts in states considered tax-friendly, such as Delaware and Nevada, to reduce their state income tax, said Lo. Retirement The financial future of Social Security looms over Washington. The election doesn’t provide a solution, but it strengthens Democrats’ hand in shaping one. Many Democrats want to build a firmer foundation for the program by raising more revenue from (i.e. taxing) high earners, rather than cutting benefits. A Democrat-led Congress is likely to pursue efforts to expand the universe of people covered by retirement plans. Representative Richard Neal, a Massachusetts Democrat and a chief sponsor of 2022’s Secure 2.0 Act, the last major retirement bill Congress passed, is set to retake the reins at the House Ways and Means Committee, one of the powerful panels with jurisdiction over retirement plans. Potentially on the docket: expanding automatic enrollment in retirement plans, increasing plan eligibility among part-time and gig workers, and possibly creating a federal retirement account for people who don't have access to a workplace plan. Democratic control of Congress will also mean a bigger hand in oversight of the Department of Labor, which houses the agency that regulates workplace retirement plans, health insurance and other employee benefits. That could mean an increased focus on strengthening participant protections and less emphasis on easing the way for alternative investments into plans such as 401(k)s. Regardless of the election outcome, financial planners advise against letting emotion drive portfolio changes. “When someone’s party or candidate loses, the future can feel riskier than it is, and fear drives big decisions: moving to cash, claiming Social Security early or abandoning a plan,” said Eileen Olson, founder of Emerald Wealth. “But big changes take time, require legislation or are often phased in or grandfathered, so there is usually time to adjust.” Investments Markets tend to like divided government, with the S&P 500 up 1.6% Wednesday, as investors embraced the prospect of a split between Congress and the White House. History suggests that optimism is warranted. Going back to 1950, the S&P 500 has delivered positive returns in the 12 months following every midterm election, regardless of which party won. Where investors may notice a bigger difference is in individual sectors, specifically in AI. Data-center buildouts may be in for greater oversight as Democrats take control in states and in Washington. Tougher oversight doesn’t make all AI stocks losers, said Omar Qureshi, managing director at Hightower Signature Wealth. Companies whose fortunes depend heavily on building more data centers — including semiconductor manufacturers, power-equipment suppliers and neocloud providers, which rent out AI computing capacity— could face more pressure. Existing data centers with secured power capacity may become more valuable as new projects get harder to build. Qureshi also sees a potential shift toward established technology companies such as Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. that can make money from AI without relying solely on an ever-faster infrastructure buildout. In health care, Democratic efforts to protect Medicaid and restore Affordable Care Act subsidies could benefit hospital operators by increasing the number of insured patients, while renewed pressure to lower drug prices and tighten Medicare Advantage rules could weigh on drugmakers and insurers, said Lale Akoner, global market strategist at eToro. Energy and Consumer Prices Gas prices jumped above $4 a gallon after the US entered the war with Iran and have largely stayed there, helping push overall inflation higher. The election brought some immediate relief in oil markets, with Brent crude tumbling nearly 9% on Wednesday as investors bet the Democratic sweep would increase pressure on Washington to wind down the conflict. Vice President JD Vance himself blamed the war for Republicans’ losses, saying voters wanted it to end. Democrats can’t end the war on their own, but they can push back on the White House’s $1.5 trillion budget request for the Pentagon and propose an oversight panel to handle investigations into the war with Iran. Gas prices began edging lower before the midterms. The national average gas price fell 12 cents to $4.12 a gallon from last week, according to GasBuddy, a fuel savings app. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a social media post that it could fall below $4 within a week. Other household costs remain high too. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Democrats could challenge Trump’s trade policies, since tariffs are another big driver of inflation. Undoing tariffs with legislation could be tough since Trump has veto power. Matt Lloyd, chief investment strategist at Advisors Asset Management, expects prices to remain elevated and said food prices could also be volatile due to El Niño’s effect on weather and crop conditions. Housing Democrats turned housing into a powerful rallying cry on their way to the midterm elections. Their new majorities in both houses of Congress will give them more power to reshape federal housing policy. But they can’t control mortgage rates, now above 7% and the biggest obstacle to easing affordability anytime soon. Some of the biggest levers to ease the housing crisis rest with Trump. His administration could seek to end the war, which is fueling inflation fears that are keeping rates high, and roll back tariffs imposed through executive action. The administration’s aggressive immigration policies are also putting pressure on builders who rely heavily on foreign-born construction workers, said Mark Zandi, chief economist of Moody’s Analytics. “The single most direct way to ease the housing affordability crisis is to end the war,” Zandi said. “There is no smoking gun, slam-dunk policy that is going to solve the problem.” The Congress passed its sweeping 21st Century Road to Housing Act designed to increase housing supply but it will take years to bear fruit. Down payment assistance proposals that some Democrats have floated would increase demand, which could in turn drive up costs in markets where supplies are limited. But what the country needs is more newly built homes that are more affordable, and that will take time and smart policy, said Susan Wachter, a real estate professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School. “We need collective action at all levels of government for a solution,” she said. “We need mortgage rates to go down and more affordable starter homes.” In Florida, voters approved sweeping property tax cuts that will begin taking effect Jan. 1. By 2028, the first $250,000 of a home's assessed value will be exempted from most property taxes. The state already has no income tax. item.title: Democrats plunge into a wide-open 2028 presidential race
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Tim Reid WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - With the US midterms over, Democrats are turning to what could become one of their most crowded and unpredictable presidential primaries in decades, a 2028 contest likely to expose the party's divide over how to win back the White House. No Democrat has emerged as a clear favorite in a field that could attract dozens of contenders, while Republicans ‌have a smaller group of widely discussed candidates, led by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to succeed President Donald Trump, who is constitutionally barred from seeking a third term. Potential Democratic ‌candidates, including sitting governors and senators, have spent months cultivating donors, visiting states with early nominating contests and raising their national profiles, positioning themselves for a race that strategists expect to begin in earnest now that the midterms are over. The sweeping victories by Democrats on Tuesday, when voters ​delivered a sharp rebuke to Trump and his agenda, will intensify discussions within both parties about how to win over an electorate unhappy with the country's direction. Despite their resounding victories on Tuesday, Democrats enter the 2028 campaign still divided over whether to tack to the center or move further left on issues ranging from healthcare and taxes to policing and foreign policy. Republican candidates will face a different challenge – how to distance themselves from Trump after Tuesday's repudiation of his policies. They need to broaden their appeal beyond the president's base while avoiding a break with the populist Make America Great Again movement that has come to define the party. Trump, who has dominated the political landscape for a decade, may be reluctant to yield center ‌stage, and his continued influence with MAGA followers could complicate the path of ⁠the party's next standard-bearer. LOOMING DEMOCRATIC BATTLE Doug Sosnik, a Democratic strategist, said both progressives and moderates will claim vindication in their ideological approaches, ensuring an intense internal battle over the party's future as the 2028 race begins in earnest. One of the most high-profile progressive wins came in the Michigan Senate contest, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed easily defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a ⁠likely 2028 presidential swing state, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. "All kinds of wings of the Democratic Party can find affirmation in the results last night," Sosnik said on Wednesday. "I don't think that anyone can, nor should they, try to contain the differences we have as a party." Several potential candidates have either acknowledged considering a White House run or declined to rule one out. Most spent the final weeks of the midterm campaign stumping for fellow Democrats in early nominating states such as Nevada, ​New ​Hampshire and South Carolina. They include former Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in 2024, Governors Gavin Newsom of California and ​Andy Beshear of Kentucky, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of ‌New York, a leading progressive voice. Reuters contacted representatives for nine of the party's most prominent potential contenders. None confirmed a 2028 run. Nine days after the November 3 elections, several prospective Democratic candidates, including Buttigieg and another progressive, US Representative Ro Khanna of California, are scheduled to attend a gathering in Denver hosted by Majority Democrats. The group, backed largely by moderate Democrats and billionaire donor Steve Mandel, advocates for younger party leaders and a party platform that is more centrist. US Representative Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts, the group's chair, said the event is meant to spark a debate about the party's future before the 2028 race takes shape, and lay out a positive agenda for what the party is for, rather than just being anti-Trump. Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist, said the party's presidential primary could attract a huge number of candidates. "There are at least 30 Democrats who are saying to people close to them, 'Do you think I should run?'" ‌Ferson said. REPUBLICANS IN TRUMP'S SHADOW By contrast, Republican 2028 hopefuls have been more guarded, mostly staying in Trump's shadow and deferential to him. That ​could now change after Tuesday night's rout in which voters expressed deep dissatisfaction with Trump's handling of the economy and foreign policy and ​demanded more action against government corruption. Vance is in a particularly difficult position, said Matt Dole, a Republican strategist. ​Vance has less freedom than other potential 2028 Republican contenders to put daylight between himself and Trump because he is vice president, a role that traditionally involves defending the president and ‌his policies. "Vance just doesn't have the wiggle room that somebody else in the cabinet ​has, who can resign," Dole said. Still, Vance acknowledged on Wednesday ​that the war in Iran, which Trump launched in February and which is deeply unpopular among Americans, had cost Republicans the election. That, however, did not represent a clear break with Trump, who made a similar acknowledgement on Tuesday night. Whoever emerges within the Republican Party as its new standard-bearer will face the task of keeping Trump's MAGA base onside while rebuilding the broader coalition that powered his 2024 victory. Exit polls ​on Tuesday showed that key constituencies of that coalition, including younger voters, Hispanics and ‌some Black men, had deserted Republicans. Vance has said there is "a chance" he will not run, citing family considerations, while Rubio has said he has "no plans at this time" to seek the presidency. Florida Governor ​Ron DeSantis, who unsuccessfully sought the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024, has declined to rule out another White House bid. Other Republicans viewed as potential candidates include Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee ​Sanders and US Senator Ted Cruz of Texas. (Reporting by Tim Reid in Washington; Editing by Ross Colvin and Howard Goller) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/midterms-over-democrats-plunge-wide-111023616.html

item.title: Republicans turn against Pete Hegseth after significant midterms losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing on Capitol Hill, on July 21. - Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images President Donald Trump may have made the decision to launch the war that tanked voters’ support for the GOP and dealt them a midterm shellacking. But the historic losses are accelerating a push for someone else to take the fall: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. And the House could vote as soon as next week to impeach the Pentagon’s top leader. Many Republican lawmakers and allies alarmed by Tuesday’s wipeout are moving swiftly to pin blame for the election results on Hegseth, arguing behind the scenes that he played a chief role in convincing Trump to attack Iran with no exit strategy — and no plan for managing the inevitable political fallout. The knives-out campaign comes despite private acknowledgement from House and Senate GOP strategists that the party’s problems extended far beyond the war, triggering 2008-level losses that will take years to reverse. But for now, party leaders – and many in their ranks – remain unwilling to directly blame Trump for their woes. Even among House Republicans who survived Tuesday’s onslaught, there’s zero expectation they will suddenly break from the president with two years left in his term. Yet that fealty does not extend to Hegseth, the combative defense secretary who has made few friends on Capitol Hill since taking over command of the Pentagon. House Republicans are expected to vote to directly repudiate the defense secretary in a matter of days. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, the famously anti-Trump GOP lawmaker, told CNN he plans to trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth when Congress returns next week — and multiple GOP sources said they expect it to pass. Rep. Thomas Massie speaks to reporters after delivering a speech introducing a proposal to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, to the House of Representatives on September 16. - Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Hegseth, a vocal cheerleader for the war, oversold the US’ ability to win the conflict quickly and easily, multiple Republicans argued to CNN, describing on condition of anonymity why many in their party are now turning against the defense secretary. They accused him of continuing to advocate for escalation despite little sign that continued bombing has brought Iran closer to surrender. The conflict has since turned into a quagmire, they said, entangling the US in the Middle East indefinitely, worsening the affordability crisis, and triggering voters’ midterm revolt against the GOP. On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance issued an extraordinary statement that “the reason we lost is the war,” though he did not assign any specific blame for the conflict. “The pivot is starting” on the war and Hegseth, a former senior Pentagon official said. “This has been primarily a Department of War-led effort because you chose to take military action to resolve a foreign policy matter.” Still, despite efforts around him to turn up the heat on Hegseth, Trump’s own confidence in his defense secretary hasn’t yet wavered even as he’s continued to survey allies about his performance, multiple White House officials told CNN. Trump personally likes Hegseth, and has told aides that he believes he should fight back against efforts to impeach him or launch investigations into his decision-making. “Just two days ago the president was in the room with him, telling him, ‘You’re my best guy. You’re the best guy I have,’” one of the officials said. Trump may also feel an additional need to keep Hegseth around if he chooses to move forward with additional strikes against Iran, another source familiar with his thinking told CNN, especially with Democrats’ new majority in the Senate likely to complicate any administration efforts to confirm new Cabinet appointees. Pressed Wednesday on Hegseth’s job status, Trump defended the war effort and denied any plans to fire him, saying he thought the defense secretary was “doing a very good job.” “If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again,” Trump said of his decision to go to war. In an interview with ABC, the president later acknowledged receiving calls from allies unhappy with Hegseth, but brushed off the complaints and vowed to keep him on. This video screenshot shows a monitor aboard the USS George Washington, displaying a camera feed of a fighter jet landing on the aircraft carrier's deck in the Arabian Sea, on September 13. The aircraft carrier was enforcing a US naval blockade against Iran. - Ed Ou/Reuters The White House also decried the prospect of Democratic investigations into the Pentagon, with spokeswoman Lauren Bis arguing in a statement that “if Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.” But some Republicans feel it may be only a matter of time before Trump looks for someone to blame for the midterm losses, and they view Hegseth as an obvious target. “If the president is serious about anyone taking responsibility for it, it’s Pete Hegseth,” one Republican close to the White House said of the electoral thrashing. “Pete has been either dishonest or incorrect — neither of which are acceptable — about timelines, goals and objectives since the beginning.” Trump has not yet signaled plans to fire any top officials. But in the aftermath of the GOP’s midterm drubbing, allies and advisers widely expect him to eventually oversee some level of changes within the administration. Within Trump’s orbit, some have seized on Hegseth’s likely impeachment as additional justification for making him the fall guy in the wake of an embarrassing rebuke of Trump’s presidency — contending that he’s bound to become a central target of Democrats’ ire over the war anyway. Hegseth, for his part, has been defiant about his ability to withstand the forthcoming wave of congressional scrutiny. While he has at times discussed his potential future ambitions with allies — including possibly running for office in Tennessee — those closest to Trump don’t believe that’s an immediate goal of his, people familiar with the discussions said. (Some Republicans on the Hill, in the meantime, privately bristle at the prospect of Hegseth serving in Congress.) In the immediate aftermath of Tuesday’s midterm election results, one person close to Hegseth told CNN that Trump’s defense secretary still expects to stay in his role and is prepared to fight an impeachment effort. Hegseth has also communicated to the White House that he’s prepared to own every policy decision and action taken by the Pentagon, the person said, believing that he’s well-equipped to defend those moves in public hearings that would likely grow contentious if Democrats launch them after they take control of Congress in January. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth walks offstage after presenting President Donald Trump during an event at Sparrows Point Shipyard, in Baltimore County, Maryland, on October 6. - Eric Lee/Reuters In a statement, chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that Hegseth “will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists.” “We will continue to drive President Trump’s agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump’s term in office,” Parnell said. Yet once that congressional scrutiny ramps up, Trump advisers and allies have questioned how long Hegseth’s resolve might last. Even before Tuesday, several White House officials, members of the president’s political operation and Trump allies candidly acknowledged the Iran war was — in their view — their biggest liability for the midterms. And Hegseth, one of the biggest proponents of military action in Iran, is intrinsically linked to that liability, they added. “I think he probably knows he’s dead but would like an exit sufficiently dramatic that it gives him a launching pad to run for POTUS,” one administration official said. For skeptics of the administration’s open-ended war in Iran, successfully pushing Hegseth out of the Pentagon would mark a critical victory — but only the first step in a broader effort to bring the fight to an end. After all, Massie noted, Trump has continued to argue for continuing the war in Iran, no matter the political and economic price paid at home. “You don’t screw up this badly an election with just one issue,” Massie said. “It was completely avoidable if they’d just broken out of the cultish following of Donald Trump.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/04/politics/pete-hegseth-impeachment-trump

US stocks fell suddenly on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday’s post-election rally. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) tumbled 2.2%, or over 1,200 points. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell 3.3%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 5%, putting the index on track to close in a correction. The PHLX Semiconductor index ( ^SOX ) dived 11% as Nvidia ( NVDA ), Micron ( MU ), and other chip names sank. Investors continued to process the Democrats' sweeping victory on Tuesday and its implications for markets and the economy . Amid relief that election uncertainty has been removed, the stock market continues to sort out the perceived winners and losers of a regime change on Capitol Hill. Oil prices rose amid uncertainty that President Trump would pursue a deal with Iran to end the war in the Middle East. item.title: Republicans call for Trump to change course as blame game begins
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Nandita Bose, Jarrett Renshaw and Bo Erickson WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump faced pressure from Republicans on Wednesday to change course after a midterm election rout handed Democrats control of Congress and voters rejected his handpicked candidates in key ‌races. Republican allies and strategists called for Trump to shake up his White House personnel, restore discipline and scrap policies they blamed ‌for the losses, including the Iran war and tariffs, as his presidency enters its final years. Veteran Republican strategist John Feehery called the results a "huge disaster" for Trump. "He needs to clean house," ​Feehery said. "Every day from this point forward, he's becoming more and more lame." But Trump showed little indication that he viewed the election outcome as a reason to change direction. "I don't view it as a hit on me," he told Fox News late on Tuesday. Democrats will now have the power to block Trump's legislation, investigate his administration and challenge his nominees. That is expected to push Trump, who has already used executive authority aggressively, toward an even greater reliance ‌on unilateral action. He will also have to decide whether ⁠to double down on an agenda that some Republicans fear has become a political liability, particularly for potential successors eyeing White House bids in 2028. Vice President JD Vance, who is viewed as Trump's likely political heir, appeared to put some ⁠distance between himself and the president on Wednesday, blaming the Iran war for the midterm losses. Such breaks could become more common if Republicans conclude Trump's longtime grip on the party's voters is weakening, strategists and party officials said. WHITE HOUSE BRACES FOR STAFF SHAKE-UP, INVESTIGATIONS Inside the White House, senior aides were bracing for ​staff departures, ​possible Cabinet changes and Democratic investigations, according to a senior official who spoke ​on condition of anonymity. "It absolutely sucks to be here right ‌now," the official said. "Morale is as low as it can get." The official said internal polling had warned six weeks before the election that Republicans were headed for losses in both chambers, but Trump refused to change course on Iran despite warnings about the political consequences. "Ultimately, he just didn't care," the official said. "He refused to listen to anyone." Trump acknowledged late on Tuesday that the eight-month-old Iran war had hurt Republican candidates but defended his decision to launch the conflict. Republican concerns extended beyond the war. In focus groups conducted for competitive Senate races in places like Michigan and Iowa, national Republican ‌political advisers grew increasingly concerned this summer as more Republican and independent voters ​voiced opposition to the president's focus on the White House ballroom and Washington renovations, a Republican ​political adviser said. "If Trump spends the next two years talking about ​this same shit, we will get shellacked again in the next election," the adviser said. Yet on Wednesday, Trump gathered ‌reporters for an impromptu visit to the ballroom construction site ​and defended the time he has ​devoted to the project. "For me it's relaxing," he said. The White House also struck a defiant public tone, posting a photograph of Trump on social media with the message: "PSA: TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT." Trump still holds considerable power. Reuters previously reported that the White House has ​spent months preparing executive actions on immigration, tariffs, ‌housing and federal spending that could allow him to advance parts of his agenda despite Democratic opposition. But executive authority will not ​be able to shield the administration from congressional probes. "Nobody wants to deal with the investigations," the official said. item.title: Steve Kornacki explains 'abrupt ending' to epic midterm marathon stream
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Steve Kornacki is back to give viewers some closure after his epic midterms marathon. The network's chief data analyst went live for a whopping 10 straight hours for NBC News' coverage of the midterm elections Nov. 3. Throughout the evening, Kornacki regularly appeared on the NBC television network to discuss the election results as they came in. But NBC also hosted a " Kornacki Cam " livestream that stayed with Kornacki all night long. The stream ended a bit abruptly, though: After impressively staying on for more than 10 hours with virtually no breaks, Kornacki told viewers he'd be taking five minutes and would be "right back," only to never return. In an early morning X post on Nov. 4 , Kornacki explained he had planned to be live for 13 hours but had to dip out a bit earlier than anticipated. "I was sure 13 hours would be fine but things caught up to me in a hurry at hour 10," he wrote. "I can't say thanks enough to all of you. What a ride and I think we did make livestream history. Sorry for the abrupt ending!" Prior to Kornacki's update, viewers had joked about the lack of closure to the stream: "I didn't want him to go without saying goodbye," one person wrote in the YouTube comments, while another quipped, "I'm not going to bed until there is proof of life from Steve." NBC's Steve Kornacki dispels a common myth about his trademark khakis At the start of Kornacki's coverage, which officially kicked off about 30 minutes before the first polls closed, the elections guru told viewers he was embarking on a "grand livestream experiment." All night, the stream would show Kornacki whenever he joined the NBC network for analysis. But in between those segments, the stream would keep on rolling continuously, so Kornacki would continue talking to viewers and providing insights. "We're doing something we've never done before," he said, explaining, "I'm going to be going into the NBC broadcast. You'll see that on this livestream. I'm going to be coming back when I'm not on NBC, and we're going to be doing results, results, results. We're going to do it all night." NBC previously utilized the "Kornacki Cam" numerous times during primary election coverage, though prior streams were typically not as lengthy or elaborate as the midterm marathon. "This started as an experiment with a House special election last year and turned into this," Kornacki wrote on X . In March, Kornacki told The Hollywood Reporter that his "Kornacki Cam" streams allow him to provide the viewer with "a much more kind of comprehensive picture of how the election was won or lost." Who is Steve Kornacki? What to know about MSNBC anchor breaking down election results Kornacki noted at the start that he was skeptical of how it would work to do a stream in the same studio where NBC anchors Savannah Guthrie and Tom Llamas would be hosting the network's regular election coverage. "When they told me they wanted to try this, I was like, 'Well, Savannah and Tom are going to want to kill me because I'm going to drive them crazy,'" he said. "But we tested the sound and everything. They said they don't really hear me. I don't really hear them." Kornacki, famed for providing incisive election analysis and breaking down results by county while standing in front of a screen dubbed the Big Board, also said early on that his plan was to keep streaming "through the morning." As the stream continued, viewers in the live chat and on social media marveled at Kornacki's stamina, especially considering he was standing the entire time and was rarely off camera for more than a few moments. Even when he wasn't speaking, the feed would usually still show Kornacki looking at his phone or a nearby monitor. "Steve's multitasking skills is legendary," one viewer commented in the live chat, and YouTuber David Doel praised the stream as possibly the "greatest thing NBC has ever concocted." At one point, after nine hours of coverage, NBC anchor Craig Melvin addressed viewers who might be confused about how Kornacki was still going. "For those of you who might be concerned about Steve Kornacki's well-being … I can confirm that Steve Kornacki has had a bathroom break, and we are nourishing him, as well." According to NBC, the "Kornacki Cam" stream was the No. 1 election live stream on YouTube for the midterms, and it amassed 29 million views across platforms. James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, becoming the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in the Lone Star State since 1988. Annie Andrews beat Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina to flip a Senate seat. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson defeated incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, putting an end to her three-decade tenure. Sen. item.title: Multiple European flights diverted after bomb threats for second time this week
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Aer Lingus plane at Evreux military air base in France after being diverted following a bomb threat [Reuters] At least 18 aircraft across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats - the second such incident this week, which the UK has called a "malicious hoax". Flights bound for Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected, including an Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome which was forced to divert to a military air base in France. Italian fighter jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome, where it landed as scheduled. No explosives have been found during searches. EasyJet said two of its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were met by Czech police after arriving in Prague as a "precautionary measure". It is not clear if the incidents are related. Follow live updates UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander described Thursday's incidents as "malicious hoax threats." She said the government was taking "these threats seriously", stressing that there were "established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats". A UK government spokesperson later said the threats reported "in the early hours" of the day had been "resolved", without giving any further details. The airport authorities in Italy's capital Rome said the hoax threat against two inbound flights received on Thursday had come by email. The warnings were signed on behalf of a group or individual calling themselves "Fighters of the Male State", claiming to be targeting a "feminist regime" and wanting to "make our mark on history". They threatened to "turn the skies red" with explosions. These details were first reported by Italian media and then confirmed to the BBC by Aeroporti di Roma, which manages both of the city airports. The following flights were targeted by threats on Thursday: Aer Lingus said its flight from Dublin to Rome diverted to Normandy, landing safely. The company added that it was working to "re-accommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible". Two Finnair flights from Helsinki landed at their destinations as normal, the airline said. One was escorted into Rome's Fiumicino airport by Italian Air Force fighter jets, Aeroporti di Roma told the BBC, while the other landed in Vienna, Austria Wizz Air said two flights which departed Milan were affected - one was heading to Warsaw, before being diverting to Vienna; the other landed safely in Bucharest, with teams inspecting the aircraft Polish airline LOT said its flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed as planned, and "no suspicious items were found". Another LOT flight from Warsaw to Paris was stopped before take-off and the plane and baggage underwent a security screening, with no hazardous items found Three Ryanair flights landed in Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian media - one from Copenhagen and another from Madrid landed in the capital Sofia, while a third coming from London bound for Sofia landed in Plovdiv. The flights were escorted by Bulgarian air force fighter jets No explosives were found on four flights which landed in Prague, Czech police said. EasyJet later said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were among those affected. "Passengers on both flights disembarked normally," the company said Aegean Airlines said it "was informed of a bomb threat" concerning two of its flights from Thessaloniki in Greece to Milan, and also from Athens to Vienna. It said threat was "unfounded", and both flights departed from the respective airports" A Ryanair flight from Porto in Portugal landed safely in Milan as planned, with bomb disposal experts checking them on arrival, Italy's Ansa news agency reported Spain's airport authority said it had received bomb threats affecting three flights at Madrid airport, but any threat was ruled out following inspections. Iberia later said two of its flights - Milan-Madrid and Rome-Madrid - were affected. It was not clear whether the third plane was the above reported Ryanair Madrid to Sofia flight Air Serbia said its flight from Belgrade to Bucharest "landed safely at its destination airport", and after checks, a reported bomb threat was "assessed as unfounded" Emily Noble, who was aboard the diverted Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome, said she was about an hour into her flight to attend a friend's wedding in the Italian capital when passengers were told about a "technical" problem. Later, as the Aer Lingus plane began circling for an unplanned landing in France, the pilot said there was a "security" issue, the 26-year-old from Dublin told BBC Verify. On board it was "an odd experience," Noble said. "It was worrying because we didn't know what was going on, but we were all trying to be as calm as we could." Noble says she could hear fighter jets during the landing and saw one touch down behind the aircraft. After landing at the Évreux-Fauville air base in Normandy, passengers learned the flight had been the subject of a bomb threat. Noble said they remained on board for two-and-a-half hours while police and military personnel carried out checks, including searches with sniffer dogs. The passengers were later told they would be taken to an airport in Paris and another plane would fly them on to Rome. Philip Baum, professor of aviation security at the University of Coventry, said the industry "faces multiple bomb threats every single day" but he had been "surprised" by this week's incidents. A flight is diverted "only when the threat is credible and the authorities believe there is a potential of explosive device on board", he said. He said the concern was that "if you issue enough hoax threats, then complacency could set in and a real threat could be ignored - or they could be a diversion". Marco Chan, an aviation expert at Kingston University, told the BBC the threats were "most likely a hoax, but the system is right to treat it as real". He said they were being viewed by some experts as "possibly part of a pattern of cheap, deniable disruption" to air travel. Hoaxes can also come from copycats, he said, but "three days of incidents is too small a sample to separate coordination from contagion". Two days ago, seven European flights, including two from the UK, were searched after bomb threats were made. No explosives were found on any of the planes after searches. On Monday, a Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia was escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.
